name: Brisk stair climb (moderate start)
duration_reps: 1 ascent of 1-3 flights (about 1-2 min) at 'can talk, not sing' pace
steps: Go to a stairwell and hold the rail. Warm up with 30 s of easy walking.
Climb at a brisk steady pace, whole foot on each step; you should be able to talk but not sing.
Walk down slowly with a hand on the rail.
Rest until you breathe normally (1-2 min). Week 1: one ascent; add one ascent per week up to 3 (adapted from the Boreham ramp, app-chosen).
key_cue: Brisk, not breathless: you can still talk.
common_mistake: Taking two steps at a time, looking at the phone, rushing the way down.
evidence_note: Moderate-intensity entry level; Boreham 2005 (RCT n=15, young women) is the only sourced ramp (1 to 5 ascents/day over 8 weeks, ~2 min each, 90 steps/min, VO2max +17.1% vs controls). Talk test per CDC/NHS. The ramp is borrowed for progression only; the app's flight count is app-chosen. Intensity note: NHS lists stair climbing as vigorous; for someone out of shape one fast flight may already be vigorous, so use the talk test and slow down if you cannot talk.

contraindications_safety: Falls risk on stairs: rail, no phone, dry stairs and sensible shoes. Avoid with knee/hip pain, vertigo or balance problems. Before starting: if you have known heart, kidney or metabolic disease (for example diabetes), or any of: chest, neck, jaw or arm pain or discomfort that could come from the heart; breathlessness at rest or with mild effort; dizziness or fainting; palpitations or a racing heart; ankle swelling; calf pain when walking; a known heart murmur; unusual tiredness or breathlessness with usual activities, check with a doctor first (ACSM 2015 / NHS). Stop at once and do not resume that day with chest pain or pressure, unusual breathlessness, palpitations or a racing/irregular heartbeat, dizziness, light-headedness or nausea; seek urgent care if it does not settle.
verification_note: Boreham 2005 re-read in Europe PMC: 15 women, mean age 18.8, 8 stair vs 7 control, 1 to 5 ascents/day, 199 steps, 90 steps/min, ~2 min, 5 d/wk, 8 wk; +17.1% VO2max relative to controls (p<0.05): CONFIRMED. Added: known-disease/symptom check before starting even moderate work (ACSM 2015: inactive people with known cardiovascular, metabolic or renal disease need clearance before starting; NHS: see GP if conditions). Added caveat that NHS classes stair climbing as vigorous, so the talk test, not the label, sets intensity for a deconditioned user. Flight counts and weekly ramp remain app-chosen.

name: Stair burst (vigorous, 20-60 s)
duration_reps: 1 burst of 20-60 s of fast climbing; 2-3 bursts/day spaced 1+ hours apart; 3 days/week; progress over weeks
steps: Only after 1-2 weeks of the moderate stair climb and only if you passed the screen.
Warm up 30 s of easy walking, hand near the rail.
Climb fast for 20-60 s (about 1-3 flights) until you can say only a few words; do not sprint two steps at a time.
Walk down slowly, rail in hand, and rest until breathing is normal. Do not stack bursts back-to-back.
key_cue: Fast enough that you can only say a few words, and always on the rail.
common_mistake: All-out sprinting on stairs; skipping steps; doing it in smart shoes or on wet stairs.
evidence_note: Trial-backed minimum: Jenkins 2019 (RCT, sedentary young adults, n=12/arm: 3 vigorous ascents of 60 steps per day, 1-4 h apart, 3 d/wk, 6 wk; VO2peak higher vs control P=0.003, gain 'modest'). Allison 2017 (3x20 s all-out ascents, 3 d/wk, 6 wk: +12% VO2peak, n=12; 3x60 s: +7%, n=11; young women only; Allison had no non-exercise control). Meta-analytic support (BJSM 2026, 11 RCTs n=414; fitness outcome g=1.37 from 6 of them, moderate certainty, I2=71%) is for supervised, mostly young adults. Babir 2026 (real-world, 58 y, type 2 diabetes, n=69, 12 wk) found NO difference in estimated VO2max. A single burst does not raise VO2max; any effect needs weeks of repetition. The trials used all-out/vigorous efforts; this entry's 'a few words' effort is a submaximal extrapolation.

contraindications_safety: Vigorous bursts: ask a doctor before starting if you have known heart, kidney or metabolic disease (for example diabetes), high blood pressure or take medicine for blood pressure or a heart condition, are pregnant, have a bone or joint problem that exercise could make worse, or have any of: chest, neck, jaw or arm pain or discomfort that could come from the heart; breathlessness at rest or with mild effort; dizziness or fainting; palpitations or a racing heart; ankle swelling; calf pain when walking; a known heart murmur; unusual tiredness or breathlessness with usual activities. If you have not been exercising regularly, build up with the moderate entries first. General information, not medical advice. Not for: knee/hip problems, vertigo, balance problems or an acute illness. Use shoes with grip, rail in hand. Stop at once and do not resume that day with chest pain or pressure, unusual breathlessness, palpitations or a racing/irregular heartbeat, dizziness, light-headedness or nausea; seek urgent care if it does not settle.
verification_note: VERIFIED against abstracts: Jenkins 2019 (Appl Physiol Nutr Metab, PMID 30649897): 3 bouts/day of vigorous ascent of a 3-flight stairwell (60 steps), 1-4 h apart, 3 d/wk, 6 wk, n=12 per arm, VO2peak higher in climbers P=0.003, 'absolute increase was modest'; the abstract gives no magnitude (a secondary French summary says ~5%, not primary; do not quote). Allison 2017 (MSSE, PMID 28009784): 31 sedentary women; 3x20 s all-out stairs 3 d/wk 6 wk: VO2peak +12% (~1 MET, P=0.002, n=12); one-flight 3x60 s: +7% (P=0.01, n=11); no control group mentioned in the abstract (pre-post). BJSM 2026 (Rodriguez et al., 60(2):133-141, PMID 41057224): 11 RCTs, n=414, snacks defined as <=5 min bouts, >=2/day, >=3 d/wk, >=2 wk; cardiorespiratory fitness g=1.37 (0.58-2.17), I2=71.4%, k=6 (only 6 of the 11 trials contributed), moderate certainty; no effect on BP, lipids or body composition. Babir 2026 (Diabetes Obes Metab, PMID 42502209): n=69, T2D not insulin-treated, mean age 58, 4x1 min vigorous, >=5 d/wk, 12 wk; the abstract lists no difference except 30-s sit-to-stand +1.9 reps (0.3-3.4). CORRECTIONS: (1) g=1.37 comes from k=6 trials, not all 11; (2) the trials used all-out or vigorous efforts, this entry asks for 'a few words' effort without sprinting, so the trial effect is not shown for this dose; (3) symptom list completed to the ACSM 2015 items (palpitations, ankle swelling, claudication, murmur added); (4) 'pregnancy beyond advice from a clinician' replaced by plain 'ask a doctor'; (5) high blood pressure or BP/heart medication now means ask a doctor (PAR-Q+ question 1/5 logic) instead of only 'uncontrolled'. Dose 3 bursts/day and 3 d/wk match Jenkins; 20-60 s duration and weekly ramp are app-chosen.

name: Brisk walk intervals (3 x 1 min)
steps: Walk at an easy pace for 30 s to warm up.
Walk briskly for 60 s: heart rate and breathing clearly up, you can talk but not sing.
Walk easy for 60 s.
Repeat 3 times, then walk easy for 30 s.
key_cue: Brisk is 'talk, not sing'.
common_mistake: Starting too fast; stopping suddenly.
evidence_note: Moderate-intensity entry level for people new to exercise (ACSM 2015: inactive people without disease/symptoms start light-to-moderate and progress gradually). Interval structure is app-chosen: no VO2 trial of this exact protocol was found. NHS lists brisk walking as moderate.

name: Fast march / low-impact high knees (30 s)
duration_reps: 2-3 x 30 s fast march with 60 s easy between, 1-3 times/day
steps: Stand tall next to the desk, one hand free to touch it for balance.
March quickly, knees to about hip height, arms swinging, feet landing softly (no jumping).
Keep going 30 s; aim to be able to say only a few words (vigorous) or full sentences with effort (moderate, start here).
Slow to an easy march for 60 s; repeat 2-3 times.
key_cue: Fast, tall and quiet: no jumping.
common_mistake: Stomping loudly, leaning back, holding the breath.
evidence_note: EXTRAPOLATION: no VO2 trial of in-place marching was found. The rationale is that exercise snacks are defined as short (<=1 min) vigorous bouts (Islam 2022 definition via search snippet; Jones 2024 scoping review) and VILPA is observational. Intensity is judged with the talk test.

name: Squat-to-calf-raise burst (30 s)
duration_reps: 1-2 x 30 s fast reps, rest 60-90 s; 1-2 times/day
steps: Stand with feet hip-width, fingertips near the desk.
Squat to a comfortable depth (thighs not below parallel), then stand fast and rise onto the toes.
Keep a quick but controlled rhythm for 30 s (about 1 rep per 1.5-2 s).
Rest 60-90 s standing; repeat once if comfortable.
key_cue: Quick up, controlled down, balance with the desk.
common_mistake: Bouncing at the bottom, knees collapsing in, heels slamming down.
evidence_note: EXTRAPOLATION. Only indirect support: Zhu 2025 (Research Square PREPRINT, not peer reviewed, n=31 students, 3 groups, NO non-exercise control: deep-squat snacks of 30-60 s, 3x/day, 3 d/wk, 6 wk; VO2peak improved within every group). It cannot show squat snacks beat doing nothing. (Re-check status: the Zhu preprint was not located in this verification pass; treat as unverified and do not cite in the app.)

name: 30-second sit-to-stand self-check
steps: Place a stable chair against a wall; sit with arms crossed over the chest.
On 'go', stand fully then sit fully as many times as you can in 30 s.
Count full stands only and write the number down.
Re-test every 4 weeks; compare to your own previous score.
key_cue: Full stand, full sit, count honestly.
common_mistake: Using the arms, half stands, a wheeled chair.
evidence_note: This measures leg function, NOT VO2max. Babir 2026 used the 30-s sit-to-stand as a secondary outcome (+1.9 reps vs control, 95% CI 0.3-3.4 after 12 weeks of 4x1 min vigorous snacks). The app should say 'functional capacity', never 'fitness age' or 'VO2'. A talk-test log (can I talk at the same brisk pace?) is a second self-check (CDC).

name: Stand, change position, shake out (45 s)
steps: Push back from the desk and stand up.
Shake out the arms and legs for 10 s, then roll the shoulders back 5 times.
Take a slow breath in, long breath out, twice, while looking across the room.
Sit down in a different position (feet flat, chair or screen adjusted) or keep standing.
key_cue: Move first, then sit differently: no single 'perfect' posture.
common_mistake: Snapping into a rigid 'military' posture and holding it.
evidence_note: Framed as 'change position and move', not 'sit up straight': Slater 2019 (expert editorial, search summary only) argues there is no strong evidence for one optimal sitting posture. Micro-break benefits in general (Albulescu 2022, via 01 notes): small improvements in fatigue (d=.35) and vigor (d=.36), no reliable performance gain.

name: Window gaze (40-60 s)
posture: seated or standing by a window
steps: Stand or lean back and look out of a window or at the farthest point you can see.
If you can see greenery or sky, rest your eyes on it; let the eyes soften instead of staring.
Breathe slowly and blink normally for 40-60 s.
Return to work and name the next small step.
key_cue: Look at the farthest and greenest thing available.
common_mistake: Checking the phone during the break.
evidence_note: Lee 2015 (n=150 students, 40 s of a green roof view vs a concrete roof, fewer omission errors; search summary only, single lab study). Looking at distant objects is also standard eye-strain advice (AAO), but the 20-20-20 timing is not supported by the one controlled test (Johnson & Rosenfield 2023, n=30, null). A later 40-s nature-view study (n=68 and n=186; PMID 35548523) found no improvement in sustained-attention performance, only that people felt more restored; treat as a pleasant pause, not a performance tool.

name: Mini muscle relaxation (75 s)
duration_reps: about 75 s: 5 areas x (5 s tense + 10 s release)
steps: Sit supported, feet flat. Make fists, tense the hands and forearms at about 50% effort for 5 s while breathing normally, then release for 10 s.
Do the same for shoulders (shrug up), then jaw (press lips together lightly), then face (scrunch), then legs (press the heels down).
Breathe out slowly with every release and notice the difference.
Finish with one slow breath out and relaxed shoulders.
key_cue: Tense gently, release fully: never hurt.
common_mistake: Tensing to maximum, holding the breath, tensing the neck hard.
evidence_note: Evidence is for multi-week PMR programmes, mostly in patient groups (Donato 2026 meta-analysis of 31 RCTs, n=2277: sleep SMD -1.74, anxiety SMD -1.11, I2 83-94%). A 75-s desk dose is UNPROVEN; the 5 s tense / 10 s release pattern is the conventional PMR rhythm and the dose is app-chosen.

name: Cool water on the face (20-30 s)
duration_reps: 20-30 s; optional, not part of the default rotation
steps: Go to a washroom and run cool (not icy) tap water.
Keep breathing normally; do not hold the breath.
Splash or hold a cold wet towel to the cheeks and forehead for 20-30 s.
Pat dry and breathe out slowly twice before sitting.
key_cue: Cool, not painful, and keep breathing.
common_mistake: Using ice-cold water, holding the breath, doing it with a medical heart-rhythm condition.
evidence_note: Richer 2022 (n=28 healthy lab participants, randomized, cold stimulus to the face after a stress task): faster HR recovery and lower cortisol response. The lab protocol is not the same as a sink splash, the sample is small and one study. Walther 2021 (n=24+24): hypertensives lacked the HR drop, so the effect is not universal. Treat as an optional comfort/alertness reset, not a stress treatment. Mechanism: cold on the face triggers the diving reflex, which slows the heart rate; for most healthy people this is mild, but it is the reason for the heart-rhythm caution. The lab used a controlled cold stimulus; a sink splash is a weaker, unmeasured version. Walther 2021 tested men only.

sources.title: Richer et al. 2022, Sci Rep: Vagus activation by Cold Face Test reduces acute psychosocial stress responses
sources.verification: abstract read via Europe PMC (PMID 36357459); n=28 healthy, randomized between-subjects, cold stimulus to the face after a lab stress task; faster HR/HRV recovery and lower cortisol response; single small lab study

sources.title: Walther et al. 2021, J Clin Med: Altered cardiovascular reactivity to Cold Face Test in essential hypertension
sources.verification: abstract read via Europe PMC (PMID 34205387); n=24 hypertensive vs 24 normotensive; 2-min cold face mask; hypertensives did not show the HR decrease

contraindications_safety: Skip with heart-rhythm problems (slow heart rate/bradycardia, irregular rhythm, pacemaker, or any heart condition: ask a doctor first, because this reflex slows the heart), high blood pressure, Raynaud's phenomenon, cold urticaria, a history of fainting, or recent face/eye injury or surgery. Use cool, not icy, water; do not hold your breath or put the face under water. Stop with dizziness, chest symptoms or palpitations.
verification_note: Richer 2022 (Sci Rep, PMID 36357459) verified: 28 healthy participants, randomized between-subjects, cold face test after MIST stress, better HR/HRV recovery and lower cortisol response. Walther 2021 (PMID 34205387) verified: 24 unmedicated hypertensive MEN vs 24 normotensive, 2-min cold face-mask, hypertensives lacked the HR decrease and diastolic BP recovery. Honest framing added: the cold face test works through the diving reflex, which slows heart rate; a sink splash without breath-hold is a much weaker stimulus than the lab protocol; effect on stress in daily life unproven. Added fainting history as a precaution (my addition, not from a source). Cardiac-rhythm caution kept and strengthened (reflex slows heart rate).

name: One-minute attention reset
steps: Put the hands down and look at one point or close your eyes.
For 60 s pay attention to the feel of breathing at the nose or belly; when the mind wanders, notice it and return.
Let one breath out be long.
Open your eyes and choose the next single task.
key_cue: Notice, return, repeat: wandering is the exercise.
common_mistake: Judging yourself for wandering; trying to force calm.
evidence_note: Workplace mindfulness evidence is for multi-week programmes with small, low-certainty effects (a 2025 review of 99 studies, N=16,054: task performance g=0.25 vs passive controls, none vs active controls, very low certainty). Balban 2023 used mindfulness as the comparator for cyclic sighing (details from repo notes). A single 60-s exercise is UNPROVEN. Kept as a quiet alternative to the existing cyclic sighing.

sources.title: Workplace mindfulness programmes meta-analysis (56 studies; stress g 0.32-0.77), Mindfulness 2020
sources.verification: abstract via search summary in research/03-interruptions-breathing.md; multi-week programmes, not micro-sessions

sources.title: Balban et al. 2023, Cell Rep Med: Brief structured respiration practices enhance mood and reduce physiological arousal
sources.verification: read in research/03-interruptions-breathing.md: n=108/100, 5 min/day x 28 days; mindfulness meditation was the comparator (+1.22 PANAS) vs cyclic sighing (+1.89); small effects

contraindications_safety: Safe for most people. People with trauma history or panic disorder can find inward attention distressing: allow eyes open and stopping any time.
verification_note: The '56 studies, g 0.32-0.77' workplace-mindfulness figure could not be verified (search summary only); the nearest retrieved review (mindfulness programmes for work performance, 99 studies, N=16,054, task performance g=0.25 vs passive control, no benefit vs active control, GRADE very low) is weaker. Removed the unverified numbers. Balban 2023 comparator numbers come from repo notes, not re-read. One-minute dose unproven; low risk.

name: Screen setup check (30 s)
duration_reps: 30 s, once a day or when strain appears
steps: Sit back in your normal working position.
Check the screen centre is about 20-28 in (50-70 cm) from your eyes and about 4-5 in (10 cm, 15-20 degrees) below eye level.
Check for glare from windows or lights on the screen; tilt the screen or lower the blinds if you see reflections.
Check text size is easy to read without leaning forward.
key_cue: Arm's length, slightly down, no glare.
common_mistake: Leaning in to read small text; screen above eye level.
evidence_note: AOA page read: 20-28 in distance, 15-20 degrees below eye level, glare control. TFOS Lifestyle 2023: optimizing the work environment may help; interventions are in general not well established. Trial evidence for ergonomic changes is limited; this is expert guidance, not a proven treatment.

sources.verification: page read via fetch-model summary: screen 20-28 in from eyes, 15-20 deg (about 4-5 in) below eye level; avoid glare from windows/overhead lights; 20-20-20 wording; blink often; annual eye exam; does NOT recommend specific eye exercises (vision therapy only for diagnosed focusing/coordination problems)

sources.verification: abstract read via Europe PMC (PMID 35597519); 45 RCTs, n=4497; no high-certainty evidence for any therapy; blue-blocking spectacles did not reduce visual fatigue (low certainty)

contraindications_safety: If you need to lean in, squint or get headaches, book an eye exam: uncorrected refractive error or presbyopia is a common cause (TFOS). Sudden vision change, pain, flashes or floaters need prompt professional care.
verification_note: AOA numbers (20-28 in, 15-20 degrees / 4-5 in below eye level) from repo page-read notes; consistent with AOA guidance. Error fixed: Singh 2022 is a Cochrane review of blue-light-filtering lenses only, so 'no high-certainty evidence for any therapy' misstated it. Opinion/expert-guidance label stands.

name: Complete-blink pause (30 s)
steps: Look away from the screen and let the face relax.
Blink fully about once every 3 s: close the lids gently all the way, then open.
Do 10 complete blinks while breathing slowly.
Return to the screen and notice your blink rate.
key_cue: Close fully, open softly.
common_mistake: Squeezing hard or fluttering rapidly.
evidence_note: AAO: normal ~15 blinks/min vs 5-7 at screens; advises conscious blinking. Xu 2025 (n=40, people WITH dry eye disease, 30 days, app-guided blink training improved blink behaviour and ocular surface measures; small, randomized vs no intervention). No trial in healthy desk workers. The existing 'blink-reset' covers a similar idea; this variant adds a paced cadence for variety.

sources.verification: page read in full (research/08): blinks ~15/min normal vs 5-7/min at screens; advises conscious blinking and looking at distant objects

sources.verification: abstract read via Europe PMC (PMID 41266739); n=40 people with dry eye disease, 30 days, randomized vs no intervention; improved blink behaviour and ocular surface measures; small, unblinded

name: Near-far focus shift (30 s)
steps: Hold a thumb at arm's length and look at it for 3 s.
Shift the gaze to something 6+ m (20 ft) away for 3 s.
Alternate near and far 5 times, blinking normally and breathing slowly.
Finish looking far for a few seconds.
key_cue: Slow, easy shifts, never forcing a blur to clear.
common_mistake: Straining or going cross-eyed to force the focus.
evidence_note: OPINION / NO ADULT TRIAL FOUND. AOA does not recommend specific eye exercises (vision therapy is for diagnosed focusing/coordination problems). Rawstron 2005 systematic review: supported mainly for convergence insufficiency, 'no clear scientific evidence' for asthenopia. Recommendation: ship only if the owner accepts an opinion-labelled item; otherwise drop. Not a Bates-method item: Bates-style 'cure' claims (palming/sunning/swinging for acuity) are excluded; eye exercises show 'limited to no efficacy' for myopia (Lin 2024).

name: Single-leg calf raise (hand on desk)
steps: Stand next to the desk, one hand resting on it for balance.
Shift your weight onto one foot, the other foot lightly off the floor behind you.
Rise up on the ball of the foot over 2 s, hold 1 s, lower over 3 s.
Finish all reps, then switch legs.
key_cue: Straight up and down, ankle stays stacked.
common_mistake: Rolling the ankle outward, bouncing, using the desk to push up.
evidence_note: Progression of the double-leg calf raise (NHS lists calf raises, 5 reps). Single-leg is the standard harder step. The ACSM 2009 stand supports progressing when the current load is easy (2-10% load, 1-2 reps above target); mapping that to 'next variation' is app-chosen. Dose is app-chosen.

name: Slow-lowering calf raise (4 s down)
steps: Stand hip-width, a hand on the desk.
Rise onto the toes in 1 s.
Lower the heels very slowly over 4 s until they just touch the floor.
Repeat 8-10 times without bouncing.
key_cue: Take 4 full seconds down.
common_mistake: Dropping the heels quickly; leaning into the desk.
evidence_note: Slow lowering is a tempo variation for variety. The Alfredson/Silbernagel eccentric protocols (e.g. Habets 2021, n=40) are rehab for people WITH Achilles tendinopathy (typically 3x15 daily) and must not be quoted as a desk dose. ACSM 2009 supports tempo control of 1-2 s up/1-2 s down for novices; the 4 s count here is app-chosen.

name: Bent-knee (soleus) calf raise
steps: Stand next to the desk, one hand on it.
Bend both knees slightly, about 30 degrees, and keep them there.
Rise onto the balls of the feet over 2 s, hold 1 s.
Lower slowly over 3 s without straightening the knees.
key_cue: Knees stay softly bent the whole time.
common_mistake: Straightening the knees at the top, which turns it into a standard calf raise.
evidence_note: Mechanics: the clinical heel-raise test uses ~0 deg knee flexion for gastrocnemius and ~30 deg for soleus (Hebert-Losier 2011, n=17, test-method paper). Use as variety, not as a proven training advantage. Dose is app-chosen.

name: Toe raises (shin/tibialis)
posture: standing with heels about 30 cm from a wall
steps: Stand with your back to a wall, heels about a foot from it, hips and shoulders touching the wall.
Keep the legs straight and lift the toes and front of the foot up toward the shins.
Hold 1 s, then lower the toes slowly over 2 s.
Repeat 10-15 times.
key_cue: Heels stay down, toes go up.
common_mistake: Bending the knees or leaning forward off the wall.
evidence_note: NO SOURCE FOUND for this specific dose or its benefit; included as the antagonist to calf raises (mechanics standard). Do not claim shin-splint prevention.

contraindications_safety: Stop with shin, ankle or front-of-ankle pain. Skip with a recent ankle or shin injury.
verification_note: No source and not a variation of a verified parent (antagonist movement to calf-raises). Very low risk and a common physio exercise, but by the ship rule it stays UNVERIFIED; owner may ship it as 'general guidance' if accepted.

name: Mini squat (hold the desk)
steps: Stand tall, feet shoulder-width, hands lightly on the desk.
Bend the knees and sit the hips back slightly, to a depth of about a quarter squat.
Pause for a second and keep the chest up.
Push through the whole foot to stand; repeat 5-8 times.
key_cue: Small and smooth: weight on the whole foot.
common_mistake: Knees caving in, heels lifting, bouncing.
evidence_note: NHS strength exercises page lists mini-squats (5 reps, 'build up slowly'). WHO/CDC: muscle-strengthening on 2+ days/week. Dose beyond 5 reps is app-chosen.

name: Bodyweight squat
posture: standing, desk in front for balance
steps: Stand with feet slightly wider than the hips, toes a little out, arms forward or hand on the desk.
Sit the hips back and down until the thighs are about parallel to the floor (or as far as is comfortable).
Keep the chest up and knees tracking over the toes; heels stay down.
Stand up over 1-2 s; repeat 8-10 times.
key_cue: Hips back, chest up, knees follow the toes.
common_mistake: Heels lifting, knees caving, rounded back.
evidence_note: WHO/CDC class-level muscle-strengthening (2+ d/wk). NHS lists mini-squats and sit-to-stand; the full-depth squat is the standard next step. Rep count is app-chosen.

name: Sumo (wide-stance) squat
steps: Stand with feet about twice shoulder-width, toes turned out 30-45 degrees.
Keep the chest up and lower the hips straight down, knees pushing out over the toes.
Go down only as far as is comfortable (thighs near parallel at most).
Squeeze the glutes as you stand; repeat 8-10 times.
key_cue: Knees follow the toes, hips go straight down.
common_mistake: Letting the knees fall inward; turning the toes out too far for the hips.
evidence_note: NO SOURCE FOUND for the wide-stance benefit; included as a stance variation of the squat (class-level WHO only). Do not claim extra glute or adductor activation.

contraindications_safety: Skip with groin, hip or knee pain; reduce turn-out if the knees hurt. Stop with sharp pain.
verification_note: Parent: bodyweight-squat. Stance variation, low risk; label now names the parent. No claim of extra glute/adductor activation made.

name: Static split squat (hand on desk)
posture: standing split stance, hand on desk
steps: Stand next to the desk and step one foot back about a long stride; hold the desk lightly.
Keep the torso upright and lower the back knee straight down toward the floor.
Stop with the front thigh near parallel and the front knee over the ankle.
Push through the front heel to rise; finish all reps, then switch legs.
key_cue: Straight down and straight up, front heel flat.
common_mistake: Leaning forward, front knee collapsing inward, stride too short.
evidence_note: NO SOURCE FOUND for this specific dose; a standard unilateral progression of the squat. Use the ACSM 2009 rule of progressing only when the easier version feels easy (adaptation is app-chosen).

name: Slow-tempo squat (3 s down)
duration_reps: 6-8 reps, 3 s down, 1 s pause, 1-2 s up
steps: Stand tall, feet shoulder-width, hand on the desk.
Lower over a count of 3 seconds to a comfortable depth.
Pause 1 second without relaxing.
Stand up over 1-2 seconds; repeat 6-8 times.
key_cue: Count three on the way down.
common_mistake: Rushing the lowering; holding the breath.
evidence_note: Tempo is a harder variation of the same squat. ACSM 2009 recommends 1-2 s concentric / 1-2 s eccentric for novices; the 3-s lowering and 1-s pause are app-chosen, not tested.

name: Squat with calf raise (slow)
steps: Stand with feet hip-width, a hand on the desk.
Squat down to a comfortable depth and pause 1 second.
Stand up and, at the top, rise smoothly onto the toes for 1 second.
Lower the heels with control and repeat 6-8 times.
key_cue: Squat first, rise second.
common_mistake: Rising onto the toes while still bent; bouncing.
evidence_level: general guidance (combination of mini-squat and calf-raises; unverified)
evidence_note: NO SOURCE FOUND; a combination of the two NHS moves (mini-squat and calf raise). For the fast cardio version see vo2-squat-calf-burst.

name: Shallow wall sit (10-20 s)
steps: Stand with your back flat against a wall, feet about 50 cm out.
Slide down only a little, knees bent about 30-45 degrees.
Hold 10-20 s while breathing normally, never holding the breath.
Slide back up and rest 20-30 s; repeat once or twice.
key_cue: Shallow and easy: keep breathing.
common_mistake: Sliding too low, holding the breath, hands pushing on the thighs.
evidence_note: Shallow, shorter variant of the existing wall-sit. Jones 2026 (n=62 healthy, mean 27 y): holding wall sit/plank to fatigue pushed 97-98% over DBP 115 mmHg after ~50 s, with no adverse events. Silva 2024 (n=17): 2-min wall squats every 30 min had no overall effect on BP or vascular function. Isometric BP-lowering evidence (Inder 2016, 11 RCTs, n=302) is for multi-week TRAINING, not a desk break. Hold cap of 20 s is app-chosen, well short of fatigue.

sources.title: Jones et al. 2026, J Hypertens: Acute blood pressure responses to plank and wall sit isometric exercise in adults
sources.verification: abstract read via Europe PMC (PMID 41252651); n=62 healthy (mean 26.7 y); held to volitional fatigue: 97-98% reached DBP >115 mmHg after ~50 s; no adverse events

sources.title: Silva et al. 2024, J Cardiopulm Rehabil Prev: Breaking up sitting with isometric wall squat, randomized crossover
sources.verification: abstract read via Europe PMC (PMID 38885063); n=17; 2-min wall squat every 30 min for 180 min; no overall effect on popliteal FMD or BP (benefit only in a subgroup)

sources.title: Inder et al. 2016, Hypertens Res: Isometric exercise training for blood pressure management, meta-analysis
sources.verification: abstract read via Europe PMC (PMID 26467494); 11 RCTs, n=302, training >=2 wk; SBP -5.20 mmHg (-6.08 to -4.33); these are multi-week isometric TRAINING programmes, not a desk-break dose

contraindications_safety: Keep holds short and breathe. Skip or check with a clinician first if you have high blood pressure, heart disease, a history of stroke or dizziness. Stop with chest pain, dizziness, headache or sharp joint pain.
verification_note: Jones 2026 verified (J Hypertens, PMID 41252651): 62 healthy adults, mean age 26.7; plank and wall sit to volitional fatigue or limit: 97% (plank) and 98% (wall sit) stopped for DBP >115 mmHg after ~50 s; all women exceeded; no SBP limit reached; no adverse events. The 10-20 s shallow hold is far below that dose. Label 'weak' implied benefit evidence; replaced by general guidance (variation of wall-sit, existing). Hypertension/heart-disease caution kept; also advise people on BP medication to ask.

name: Wall push-up
steps: Stand about an arm's length plus one step from a wall, feet hip-width.
Place hands on the wall at chest height, slightly wider than the shoulders.
Bend the elbows to about 45 degrees from the body and bring the chest toward the wall over 2 s.
Press away over 1-2 s; keep the body in one line.
key_cue: One straight line, elbows at 45 degrees.
common_mistake: Sagging hips, flaring elbows, head poking forward.

name: Standing glute squeeze
steps: Stand tall, feet hip-width.
Squeeze both glutes as if holding a coin between them, without tilting the pelvis forward.
Hold 5 s while breathing normally.
Release fully for 3 s; repeat 8-10 times.
key_cue: Squeeze and keep breathing.
common_mistake: Arching the lower back, holding the breath.
evidence_note: NO SOURCE FOUND for this dose; a basic isometric contraction (class-level WHO only).

name: Standing sideways leg lift
steps: Stand tall next to the desk, one hand resting on it.
Keep the supporting leg slightly soft and the toes of the lifting leg pointing forward.
Lift the other leg out to the side about 30-45 cm, slowly, without leaning.
Lower under control; do all reps, then switch legs.
key_cue: Straight up the side, torso stays still.
common_mistake: Leaning the trunk, swinging the leg, rolling the foot out.
evidence_note: NHS strength exercises page lists the sideways leg lift: 'raise and lower each leg 5 times'. Rep range above 5 is app-chosen.

name: Single-leg balance (fingertips on desk)
posture: standing, fingertips on a fixed desk
steps: Stand tall next to the desk with fingertips resting on it, feet hip-width.
Shift your weight onto one foot and lift the other slightly off the floor.
Hold 10-20 s, looking at a spot straight ahead.
Lower and switch legs; repeat twice.
key_cue: Look at one still point; breathe.
common_mistake: Gripping the desk, hiking the hip, looking down at the feet.
evidence_note: Exercise programmes with balance and strength training reduce falls in people aged 60+ (Sherrington 2019 Cochrane: 108 RCTs, 23,407 people, mean age 76, rate ratio 0.77, high certainty). That evidence is in OLDER adults; for office workers use as proprioception variety only. Single-leg stance time declines with age (Springer 2007, n=549).

name: Single-leg balance (no hand)
posture: standing near (not holding) a fixed desk
steps: Stand tall within arm's reach of a fixed desk, hands crossed at the chest or hovering.
Lift one foot slightly and balance, eyes on a fixed point.
Hold 10-30 s; touch the desk any time you lose balance.
Switch legs; progress later to a softly bent knee (not eyes closed).
key_cue: Eyes on a spot, soft knee.
common_mistake: Closing the eyes too early, locking the knee.
evidence_note: Same evidence as the supported version (Sherrington 2019 is in 60+ adults). Eyes-closed variants are deliberately excluded for desk use.

name: Wall push hold (isometric, 10 s)
steps: Stand an arm's length from a wall and place hands at shoulder height.
Lean in with elbows bent about 90 degrees and hold the position, pushing gently into the wall.
Keep the body in one line and breathe normally for 10 s.
Step back and rest 20 s; repeat 3 times.
key_cue: Gentle push, steady breathing.
common_mistake: Holding the breath, shrugging the shoulders, bracing at maximum effort.
evidence_level: general guidance (isometric variation of wall-push-up; unverified)
evidence_note: NO SOURCE FOUND for this exact hold. Isometric training lowers BP only as multi-week programmes (Inder 2016: 11 RCTs, n=302, SBP -5.2 mmHg). Jones 2026: sustained isometric holds to fatigue raised DBP past 115 mmHg in most healthy young adults; the 10-s hold is app-chosen and far shorter.
